title: Invented Style
bigQuestion: When a film makes a style famous, who decides what that style's name means in a real school?

story.title: A Name From the Screen
story.kicker: A new student asks a teacher for an art that exists mostly in movies.
paragraphs: In the middle of the 1980s, parents across the United States walked into small karate schools with a new request. Their children had seen a movie, and they wanted to learn what the hero learned. Many of them named a ninja, a fictional dojo, or a teacher who existed only on screen.

The teachers in those rooms usually belonged to real lines. Some traced their training to Okinawan teachers, some to Japanese university clubs, and some to Korean federations. Their certificates named places and people. The movies named characters, villains and invented schools with dramatic names.

Studios chose names that sounded good in a trailer. Schools, by contrast, chose names tied to a teacher, a town or an association. When a hit film reached theaters, those two ways of naming ran into each other at the front desk of a strip-mall gym.

Historians study that meeting. They ask where a style's name first appears, in a record or in a script, and what happened to real schools after the film came out. This chapter follows that question from wartime Japan to Bangkok, Jakarta and suburban America.
story.think: If a film invents a school's name and a real gym then adopts it, is the style invented, real, or both?

lessons.title: Kurosawa's Judo Film
lessons.mainIdea: Akira Kurosawa's first film, Sanshiro Sugata (1943), turned the early rivalry between judo and older jujutsu schools into a screen drama.
reading: Akira Kurosawa directed his first feature film, *Sanshiro Sugata*, in Japan in 1943. It was based on a 1942 novel by Tsuneo Tomita. Tomita's father had trained at the Kodokan, the judo school that Kanō Jigorō founded in Tokyo in 1882. Kurosawa went on to direct Seven Samurai in 1954.

The film is set in the 1880s, when judo competed with older *jujutsu* schools for students and police contracts. The hero was loosely modeled on Saigō Shirō, an early Kodokan student. The story shrinks years of real rivalry into a few dramatic contests between invented characters.

Japan was at war when the film opened, and government censors reviewed every movie. Wartime officials favored stories that praised discipline and Japanese tradition. The film is now read as evidence of two eras at once: the 1880s it shows and the 1940s that made it.

words.d: Akira Kurosawa's 1943 film about a young judo student in the 1880s
a group of older Japanese grappling schools that judo grew out of and competed with
the judo school and headquarters that Kanō Jigorō founded in Tokyo in 1882

look.title: Two Dates in One Film
look.text: A film made in 1943 shows a judo contest set in the 1880s. The costumes, the police officers and the rival schools come from the 1880s. The script, the censors' approval and the idea of what a hero should be come from 1943.
look.prompt: Name one thing a historian could learn about the 1880s from this film and one thing about the 1940s.

check.q: What was Sanshiro Sugata based on?
check.why: Kurosawa adapted Tsuneo Tomita's 1942 novel for his 1943 film.

check.q: Which real rivalry does the film dramatize?
check.why: The film is set in the 1880s, when the Kodokan competed with older jujutsu schools.

check.q: Why is the film evidence of the 1940s as well as the 1880s?
choices: Wartime censors and values shaped how it was made
check.why: The film was made under wartime review, so its script reflects 1943 as well as the era it shows.

lessons.title: The Ninja on Stage and Screen
lessons.mainIdea: Historical shinobi were spies and scouts, while the black-clad ninja of film grew largely from theater and later popular fiction.
reading: Records from Japan's Sengoku period, the age of warring states from the late 1400s to about 1600, mention *shinobi*. They were hired scouts, spies and raiders. Many came from the Iga and Kōga areas, in today's Mie and Shiga prefectures. Warlords of the period hired them to gather news about rival armies.

The black suit most people picture came later. Many historians link it to *kabuki* theater, where stagehands dressed in black so the audience would treat them as unseen. Novels, comics and films of the twentieth century then turned the ninja into a superhero with a uniform.

The 1967 James Bond film You Only Live Twice showed a ninja training camp to world audiences. In 1981 Enter the Ninja, starring Japanese-born actor Sho Kosugi, helped start an American ninja boom. The comic Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, created by Kevin Eastman and Peter Laird in 1984, carried the word to children.

words.d: an older Japanese word for the scouts and spies of the warring-states era
Japan's age of warring states, from the late 1400s to about 1600
a form of Japanese stage drama that grew from the early 1600s

look.title: Spy or Superhero
look.text: One description: a hired scout from Iga slips into an enemy castle town, dressed like a farmer, and reports what he sees. A second description: a figure in a black mask leaps over rooftops at midnight and fights ten guards at once.
look.prompt: Which description fits the historical records better, and where did the second one likely come from?

check.q: Which areas are most linked to historical shinobi?
check.why: Records tie many shinobi to the Iga and Kōga areas of central Japan.

check.q: Where do many historians trace the ninja's black suit?
check.why: Kabuki stagehands wore black to be treated as unseen, and many historians link the costume to them.

check.q: Which 1981 film helped start an American ninja boom?
check.why: Enter the Ninja, starring Sho Kosugi, came out in 1981.

lessons.title: The Karate Kid in 1984
lessons.mainIdea: The 1984 film The Karate Kid gave its teacher an Okinawan home and its villains an invented dojo, and both names spread to real schools.
reading: *The Karate Kid* opened in the United States in June 1984. It was directed by John G. Avildsen. Pat Morita played Mr. Miyagi, a maintenance worker from Okinawa who teaches a teenager from New Jersey living in California. Ralph Macchio played the teenager, Daniel.

The film tied its hero's karate to Okinawa, which matches the real history of the art in the Ryukyu Islands. Its rival school, *Cobra Kai*, was invented for the script. The film's martial arts advisor, Pat E. Johnson, was a real American karate teacher and referee.

Karate schools across the country reported more young students after the film. The movie had sequels, and a series called Cobra Kai began in 2018. A fictional dojo name thus lived on for more than thirty years without ever having a real founder. Its creators had grown up watching the original films.

words.d: a 1984 American film about a teenager who learns karate from an Okinawan teacher
the invented rival dojo in The Karate Kid, later the title of a television series
a person hired by a film to plan and check how fight scenes look

look.title: Real Island, Invented Room
look.text: In the film, Mr. Miyagi's karate comes from Okinawa. The villains' dojo, Cobra Kai, has a snake logo and a harsh motto. Okinawa appears on real maps and in real teaching lines. Cobra Kai appears only in scripts and on licensed products.
look.prompt: Which part of the film matches documented karate history, and which part does not?

check.q: Where is Mr. Miyagi from in The Karate Kid?
check.why: The film makes Mr. Miyagi an Okinawan, matching karate's real roots in the Ryukyu Islands.

check.q: What was Cobra Kai?
choices: an invented dojo written for the film
check.why: Cobra Kai was created for the 1984 script and later became a series title.

check.q: What did Pat E. Johnson do for the film?
choices: He served as martial arts advisor
He wrote the novel it was based on
check.why: Pat E. Johnson, a real karate teacher and referee, was the film's martial arts advisor.

lessons.title: A Title Keeps Its Word
lessons.mainIdea: The 2010 remake of The Karate Kid kept the word karate in its title even though its story is set in Beijing and shows Chinese martial arts.
reading: In 2010 Columbia Pictures released a new *The Karate Kid*. Jaden Smith played an American boy who moves to Beijing. Jackie Chan played Mr. Han, a maintenance man who teaches him Chinese martial arts. The film was a new version of the 1984 story, set in a different country. Its fights were planned with Chinese martial arts in mind.

Inside the film, characters call the art kung fu, and karate is a Japanese and Okinawan art. The title kept the famous 1984 word anyway. In China the film was released under a Chinese title that means roughly kung fu kid, and several other countries also used a kung fu title.

The case shows a *brand* at work. A brand is a name a company owns and sells because audiences already know it. Studios kept the name for its market value, while the story inside the film pointed to a different tradition and a different country. Audiences in each country saw the name they were most likely to buy.

words.d: a new film made from the story of an older film
a name a company owns and sells because buyers already know and trust it
a common English name for many different Chinese martial arts

look.title: One Film, Two Titles
look.text: A 2010 film follows a boy who learns a Chinese art in Beijing. In the United States the poster says The Karate Kid. In China the poster uses a Chinese title about a kung fu kid.
look.prompt: Why might one studio sell the same film under two different martial arts names?

check.q: Where is the 2010 Karate Kid set?
check.why: The remake moves its story to Beijing.

check.q: What does the word brand mean in this lesson?
choices: a name a company owns and sells because buyers know it
check.why: The studio kept the Karate Kid name because audiences already knew it.

check.q: Which art do characters in the 2010 film call their practice?
check.why: The film shows Chinese martial arts, which characters call kung fu, despite the title.

lessons.title: Ong-Bak and Muay Boran
lessons.mainIdea: The 2003 Thai film Ong-Bak sold muay boran to world audiences and sent new visitors looking for the older Thai art.
reading: *Ong-Bak* opened in Thailand in 2003. Prachya Pinkaew directed it, and Tony Jaa played a young villager who travels to Bangkok. The plot follows him as he tries to recover the stolen head of his village's Buddha statue. The village in the story is in Thailand's northeast, the Isan region.

The film advertised *muay boran*, the older Thai fighting styles that came before modern ring Muay Thai. Its marketing stressed that stunts were done without wires or computer effects. That claim became part of how the film sold itself abroad. Tony Jaa had trained for years as a stunt performer before the role.

After the film spread overseas, some gyms outside Thailand began to add muay boran to their signs. Thai teaching camps had long passed on older forms within families and regional lines. The film did not create those lines, but it gave their name a new international market.

words.d: a 2003 Thai action film starring Tony Jaa
a Thai name for older styles of boxing that came before modern ring Muay Thai
a dangerous-looking action filmed for a movie, often by a trained performer

look.title: A Sign After a Film
look.text: A gym in Europe hung a sign reading Muay Thai for years. After 2003 it added a second line: and Muay Boran. The coaches had trained in ring Muay Thai. A new student points at the second line and names Ong-Bak.
look.prompt: What questions would a historian ask about the second line on the sign?

check.q: Who starred in Ong-Bak?
check.why: Tony Jaa played the lead in the 2003 Thai film.

check.q: What is muay boran?
choices: a name for older Thai boxing styles
check.why: Muay boran means ancient boxing and names older styles before modern ring Muay Thai.

check.q: Which statement about Ong-Bak and muay boran is accurate?
choices: The film gave an older name a new world market
Thailand banned the name after the film
check.why: Older forms existed in Thai teaching lines; the film spread the name abroad.

lessons.title: Silat in The Raid
lessons.mainIdea: The Indonesian films Merantau (2009) and The Raid (2011) brought pencak silat to world screens through a Welsh director and Indonesian performers.
reading: Welsh director Gareth Evans moved to Indonesia and filmed a documentary about *pencak silat*, the Indonesian family of martial arts. There he met Iko Uwais, a young silat practitioner from Jakarta. Evans cast him in the film *Merantau*, released in 2009.

Their next film, The Raid, was released in 2011 and reached international theaters in 2012. Its fights were designed with Uwais and fellow silat practitioner Yayan Ruhian. Reviewers abroad often introduced silat to readers who had never heard the word.

Merantau takes its title from a Minangkabau custom in West Sumatra, where young men leave home to gain experience. Silat's real history runs through many regions and peoples of Indonesia, Malaysia and nearby lands. One film shows one urban action style, not the whole family.

words.d: the Indonesian name for a large family of martial arts from the Malay world
a Minangkabau custom in which young men leave home to gain experience
a people of West Sumatra, Indonesia

look.title: Years Films Put a Named Art on Screen
look.cite: Release dates from the films' credits and national film records
look.prompt: How many years passed between the first and the last film on this list?

check.q: Who directed Merantau and The Raid?
check.why: Welsh director Gareth Evans made both films in Indonesia.

check.q: Where does the word merantau come from?
choices: a Minangkabau custom of leaving home to gain experience
check.why: Merantau is a Minangkabau custom in West Sumatra.

check.q: Why can't one film stand for all of silat?
choices: Silat is only a film style
Silat is a large family of arts from many regions and peoples
check.why: Pencak silat names many arts across Indonesia, Malaysia and nearby lands.

lessons.title: Choreographers Cross the Pacific
lessons.mainIdea: Hong Kong fight choreographers such as Yuen Woo-ping carried their film methods to Hollywood in The Matrix (1999) and Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon (2000).
reading: A fight *choreographer* designs how a screen fight looks, much as a dance choreographer plans a dance. Yuen Woo-ping built his career in the Hong Kong film industry from the 1970s. He was known for *wire work*, where performers hang on hidden cables for leaps.

The Wachowskis hired Yuen to design the fights in *The Matrix*, released in 1999. The actors trained for months before filming. The film's success made Hong Kong methods a standard part of Hollywood action films. It earned hundreds of millions of dollars around the world, and two sequels followed in 2003.

Yuen also designed the fights for Ang Lee's Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon in 2000. It won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film. Many viewers abroad began to use its screen movement as their picture of Chinese martial arts, though it was a designed performance.

words.d: a person who designs how a dance or a screen fight looks
filming performers on hidden cables so they appear to leap or fly
a 1999 American science fiction film with fights designed by Yuen Woo-ping

look.title: A Credit Line
look.text: At the end of an American film, the credits list a director, a writer, a composer and a fight choreographer from Hong Kong. The fights on screen look nothing like a school class. They were planned shot by shot for a camera.
look.prompt: What does the credit line tell a historian about where the film's fight style came from?

check.q: What does a fight choreographer do?
choices: designs how a screen fight looks
check.why: A choreographer designs the look of a screen fight, as a dance choreographer plans a dance.

check.q: Which 1999 film hired Yuen Woo-ping?
check.why: The Wachowskis hired Yuen to design The Matrix's fights.

check.q: What award did Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon win?
choices: the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film
check.why: Ang Lee's 2000 film won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film.

lessons.title: Karate Arrives in America
lessons.mainIdea: Karate schools opened in the United States after World War II, and magazines and tournaments built a market before the film boom.
reading: American servicemen stationed in Okinawa and Japan after World War II trained in local karate schools. Some came home and opened schools of their own. Robert Trias, a Navy veteran, is widely credited with opening one of the first karate schools in the United States, in Phoenix, Arizona, in 1946.

*Black Belt* magazine began publishing in 1961. It printed school listings, interviews and tournament results. For many Americans far from Okinawa, the magazine was the first written record of teachers and lines they could check. Its covers and advertisements also shaped what readers expected karate to look like.

Ed Parker, a teacher from Hawaii, held the first Long Beach International Karate Championships in California in 1964. Tournaments like it gave American karate a public stage before Hollywood did. When films later drove new students to schools, a network of teachers, magazines and events was already in place.

words.d: a member of the armed forces
an American martial arts magazine first published in 1961
a planned series of contests that ends with a winner

look.title: Early American Karate Milestones
rows: Trias opens a school in Phoenix
look.cite: Black Belt magazine records; Long Beach International Karate Championships records
look.prompt: How many years of schools, magazines and tournaments came before The Karate Kid?

check.q: How did many Americans first meet karate after World War II?
choices: while stationed in Okinawa and Japan as servicemen
check.why: Servicemen trained in local schools while stationed in Okinawa and Japan.

check.q: When did Black Belt magazine begin?
check.why: Black Belt magazine began publishing in 1961.

check.q: Who held the first Long Beach International Karate Championships?
check.why: Ed Parker held the first Long Beach event in 1964.

lessons.title: Kajukenbo: A Documented New Style
lessons.mainIdea: Kajukenbo, founded in Hawaii in 1947, shows how a new style can have a real, recorded beginning instead of an invented legend.
reading: Not every new style comes from a film. *Kajukenbo* began in 1947 at the Palama Settlement in Honolulu, Hawaii. Five teachers from different backgrounds worked together to build it. The Palama Settlement was a community center serving working families of many backgrounds.

The name combines parts of the arts its founders brought: karate, judo and jujutsu, Kenpo, and Chinese boxing. Hawaii's plantation history had brought together Japanese, Chinese, Filipino, Korean and Native Hawaiian families. The style's mixed name reflects that mixed neighborhood.

Kajukenbo schools keep records of the founders and their students. That kind of *lineage*, a documented chain of teachers, is what historians look for. A style can be new and still be real when its founding place, date and people are on record. The Kajukenbo name is still used by schools in Hawaii and on the mainland.

words.d: a style founded in Honolulu in 1947, named for the arts its founders combined
a documented chain of teachers and students
a community center in Honolulu where Kajukenbo began

look.title: Two Kinds of New
look.text: Style A: founded in Honolulu in 1947 by five named teachers, with its history kept by its schools. Style B: first seen in a 1980s movie as the name of a villain's dojo, with no founder but a screenwriter.
look.prompt: Both styles are new. What makes one a documented style and the other a film invention?

check.q: Where and when did Kajukenbo begin?
check.why: Kajukenbo began at the Palama Settlement in Honolulu in 1947.

check.q: What does Kajukenbo's name come from?
choices: parts of the arts its founders brought
check.why: The name joins parts of karate, judo and jujutsu, Kenpo and Chinese boxing.

check.q: What does lineage mean?
choices: a documented chain of teachers and students
check.why: Lineage is the recorded chain of teachers that historians look for.

lessons.title: Tae Bo and the Trademark
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1990s Tae Bo turned martial arts names into a trademarked fitness program sold on video.
reading: Billy Blanks, an American karate competitor, created *Tae Bo* in the 1990s. The name blends taekwondo and boxing. It was a workout set to music, not a combat art or a competitive sport. Blanks had competed in karate tournaments in the 1970s and 1980s. He had also worked in films as a performer.

Blanks sold Tae Bo on home videos and through television ads, and it became hugely popular by the late 1990s. Blanks registered Tae Bo as a *trademark*. A trademark is a name protected by law, so others may not sell products under it without permission.

Gyms soon offered classes with generic names like cardio kickboxing. Those classes borrowed the look of martial arts for fitness. Historians see Tae Bo as a case where a martial arts name became a legal product, owned by one person, rather than a lineage.

words.d: a 1990s fitness program by Billy Blanks, named from taekwondo and boxing
a name or sign protected by law so only its owner can sell products under it
a general name that no one owns

look.title: Three Class Names
look.text: A gym schedule lists three classes: Tae Bo, cardio kickboxing and Okinawan karate. One name belongs to a company. One is a general fitness label. One names a place and points to teaching lines.
look.prompt: Match each class name to the kind of claim it makes.

check.q: What two names does Tae Bo blend?
check.why: Tae Bo joins parts of taekwondo and boxing.

check.q: What is a trademark?
choices: a name protected by law so only its owner can sell under it
a rank in a karate school
check.why: Blanks registered Tae Bo as a trademark, a legally protected name.

check.q: How did Tae Bo differ from a lineage art?
choices: It had many founders over centuries
It was a trademarked fitness program owned by one person
check.why: Tae Bo was a legal product for fitness, not a chain of teachers.
